title: Mary across the churches
hook: churches call Mary God-bearer; Catholics and Orthodox honor her highly; Protestants honor her as a model disciple

segments.voice: Yesterday, other views of the table: in, with and under; fed by the Spirit; a meal of memory. Your line was do this in memory. Did you wait for someone before you ate? Day one thousand one hundred three.

A young woman hurries into the hill country of Judea to see her cousin Elizabeth. Her name is Mary, and she is carrying news she can hardly explain. She barely gets through the door. Elizabeth, old and herself unexpectedly pregnant, cries out: "And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" The mother of my Lord. Christians have thought hard about that phrase. Today, how the churches honor Mary, and the Greek title that stands behind much of it. Today's word: Theotokos.

Theotokos is Greek for God-bearer: the one who gave birth to God. That sounds bold, and it's meant to. But the title is really about her son. If the child she carried is one person, truly God and truly human, then the woman who bore him bore God. When this was argued in the early church, a council at Ephesus defended the title, and Orthodox and Catholic prayer still uses it. From there the churches honor her in different ways. Orthodox Christians sing hymns to the Theotokos and keep her icons close. Catholics pray the Hail Mary and the rosary, and teach that she was conceived without sin and taken up body and soul into heaven. Protestant churches generally don't pray to her, and don't hold those last teachings as doctrine. They honor her as the model disciple: the one who heard God's word and said, "be it unto me according to thy word." At a wedding in Cana, when the wine ran out, she turned to the servants and said: "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it." She points away from herself, to him. Then there's her own song in Luke, the Magnificat. It begins: "My soul doth magnify the Lord, and my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." And a few lines later, the line that gives today its carry: "from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed." A young woman from Nazareth says that about herself. Whatever a church teaches about her, that sentence is in its Bible. The churches argue over how to honor her. None of them disputes that she is blessed.

Here's the practice: read the Magnificat. It's Mary's song, in Luke chapter one, starting at verse forty-six. Find it in any Bible, or on your phone, and read it slowly, once. Notice who goes up in the song and who comes down: the proud scattered, the mighty put down from their seats, the lowly lifted, the hungry filled. Then let the reading go, and sit with whichever line stays. If you pray, you can let her words rise as your own for a moment. If you don't, just let the song be heard. The bell holds the time.
Theotokos. Greek for God-bearer: Mary, the mother of the child Christians call truly God and truly human.
Your line: all generations call her blessed. Today, notice one ordinary person whose yes made room for something good, and tell them so. Day one thousand one hundred three.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Hail Mary and the rosary; Orthodox Christians sing hymns to the Theotokos in their services; Protestant churches read Mary's song, the Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55), and honor her as a model of faith, especially around Christmas.

notes: Index hook says 'most churches call Mary God-bearer' and 'many Protestants'; per the claims rule the script avoids the counts. Suggest the index hook drop 'most' and 'many' (this script's hook field does).
Council of Ephesus mentioned without a date; confirm 'churches East and West have kept it' is acceptable (some Protestant confessions accept the title formally; others rarely use it).

Catholic teachings named: Immaculate Conception and Assumption; Orthodox hold the Dormition and use different language. Confirm 'Protestant churches don't pray to her, and don't hold those last teachings' is fair (some Anglicans and Lutherans vary).
Elizabeth described as 'old' (Luke 1:36 'in her old age'); Mary is from Nazareth (Luke 1:26–27). Confirm.
